source_text:
Γύμνασον ἐν λογισμοῖς τοὺς ὁπλίτας, οἳ ἐμπείρως ἔχουσι πρὸς τὴν μάχην· καὶ δεῖξον φοβερὸν
τὴν ἧτταν τῇ ἀπειλῇ τῆς αἰωνίου κολάσεως. Τὸν νικητὴν ἀνακήρυττε λαμπροῖς ἐπαίνοις, οἶδε γὰρ καὶ ἡ εὐφημία σπουδαιοτέρους ποιεῖν· καὶ τὸν ἐπηρεασθέντα θεράπευσον συμπαθῶς, οὐχ ἧττον γὰρ ἀπειλῆς ἐντρέπει συγγνώμη τὸν συνετόν. Μὴ κινήσῃ θυμῷ ἐφ' ἁμαρτήσαντι μαθητῇ, οὐ γὰρ ὅσιον ἑαυτὸν τιτρώσκειν πρὸ τῆς θεραπείας ἑτέρου· ἀλλὰ ἀνεξικάκως διόρθωσαι πρὸς τὸ ἀγαθόν· καὶ γὰρ ἰατρὸς θεραπεύει μὲν τὸ πάθος, οὐκ ἀγανακτεῖ δὲ πρὸς τὸν ἀκουσίως νοσήσαντα. Τέμνων ἰατρός, χωρὶς ὀργῆς τοῦτο ποιεῖ· καὶ ἐλέγχων διδάσκαλος μὴ μιγνύτω τῷ ἐλέγχῳ θυμόν.
thought_title: Training, praise, and correction without anger
orientation: Evagrius is addressing the monastic leader directly, continuing his instructions on how to equip and guide disciples in spiritual combat.
pass_a_gloss: Train in thoughts the soldiers, who have experience toward the battle; and show fearful the defeat by the warning of eternal punishment. [Note: 'leader' = teacher = shepherd = pilot = general = physician.] Proclaim the victor with bright praises, for praise also knows how to make people more zealous; and heal the one who has been mistreated with sympathy, for forgiveness brings the sensible person to shame no less than warning. [Note: all terms refer to community members under guidance.] Do not be moved with anger at a disciple who has sinned, for it is not holy to wound oneself before the healing of another; but correct patiently toward the good; for a physician heals the suffering, but does not get angry at the one who has fallen ill involuntarily. A physician cutting does this without anger; and a teacher reproving, let him not mix anger with the reproof.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the dative plural; the training is in the realm of thoughts or reasonings, not physical exercise.

choices.english: by the warning of eternal punishment
choices.why: Glossary requires 'warning' for ἀπειλή; the genitive chain is kept literal.
rejected: by the threat of eternal punishment

choices.why: The comparative adjective with ποιεῖν is rendered literally; the implied object is people in general.

choices.english: the one who has been mistreated
choices.why: Passive participle of ἐπηρεάζω, meaning one who has suffered insult or mistreatment; kept literal.
rejected: the one who has been wronged

choices.why: The adverb means bearing evil patiently, without resentment; 'patiently' captures the sense without over-translating.

choices.english: the one who has fallen ill involuntarily
choices.why: The aorist participle of νοσέω with the adverb ἀκουσίως is rendered literally to preserve the point that illness is not chosen.
rejected: the one who became sick unwillingly

pass_b_english: Train your soldiers in their thoughts, so that they are skilled for battle, and make defeat a fearful thing by the warning of eternal punishment. Proclaim the victor with shining praises, for praise also knows how to make people more zealous. And heal the one who has been wounded with compassion, for forgiveness shames the sensible person no less than a warning does. Do not be moved to anger against a disciple who has sinned, for it is not holy to wound your own soul before healing another. Instead, correct him patiently toward the good. For a physician heals the disease and does not grow angry with the one who has fallen ill involuntarily. When a physician cuts, he does it without anger; and when a teacher corrects, let him not mix anger into the correction.

problems.quote: the one who has been mistreated
problems.why: ἐπηρεασθέντα means 'the one who has been wounded/hurt in battle', not 'mistreated'.
problems.fix: the one who has been wounded

edits.old: the one who has been mistreated
edits.new: the one who has been wounded

problems.why: Single role called by six different titles; reader may not see unity.
problems.fix: Add note: 'leader' = teacher = shepherd = pilot = general = physician.

problems.why: Those led are called disciples, brothers, soldiers, monks interchangeably.
problems.fix: Note: all terms refer to community members under guidance.

problems.quote: A physician heals the disease, after all, and does not grow angry
problems.why: Author's voice or quoted maxim? Unclear if proverb or author's argument.

problems.quote: forgiveness shames the sensible person no less than a warning does
problems.why: Forgiveness 'shames'? Unexpected; normally praise or warning motivates, forgiveness relieves.
problems.fix: Check Greek: may mean 'brings to shame' i.e., makes one feel ashamed before kindness.

problems.quote: heal the one who has been wounded with compassion
problems.why: Wound-healing metaphor shifts between sections without signaling it is the same medical analogy.
problems.fix: No change needed if metaphor is self-evident; could add a brief note.

variants.text: heal him quickly once he is wounded
heal the one who has been wounded with compassion

problems.quote: make defeat a fearful thing by the warning of eternal punishment
problems.why: 'Warning' appears as both a technical term and a common word in the same section; intro lists it as a key term.

problems.quote: for it is not holy to wound yourself before healing another
problems.why: 'Wound yourself' is puzzling: does anger at a disciple's sin wound the leader spiritually? The metaphor needs unpacking.
problems.fix: Clarify that anger harms the leader's own soul, so he is 'wounded' before he can help.

edits.old: for it is not holy to wound yourself before healing another.
edits.new: for it is not holy to wound your own soul before healing another.

edits.old: A physician heals the disease, after all, and does not grow angry with the one who has fallen ill involuntarily.
edits.new: For a physician heals the disease and does not grow angry with the one who has fallen ill involuntarily.

fixed: The glossary note for 'leader' is added to the literal gloss, not the English, as requested.
The glossary note for 'disciple' is added to the literal gloss, not the English, as requested.
The speaker issue is resolved by making the physician analogy explicitly the author's explanatory analogy with 'For'.
The mistranslation of 'forgiveness shames' is corrected to 'brings the sensible person to shame' in the gloss, matching the Greek sense of making one feel ashamed before kindness.
The wound-healing metaphor is self-evident; no change needed.
The 'warning' term is contextually clear; no change needed.
The 'wound yourself' metaphor is clarified by adding 'your own soul' to show the leader harms himself spiritually.

last_rejected.quote: forgiveness shames the sensible person no less than a warning does
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐχ ἧττον γὰρ ἀπειλῆς ἐντρέπει συγγνώμη τὸν συνετόν
last_rejected.why: English says 'no less than' = 'equally or more', but source says 'not less than' = 'at least as much as'. Actually these are equivalent. Wait: 'no less than' means 'at least as much as', which matches 'οὐχ ἧττον' (not less). Correct.
last_rejected.ruling: Reporter self-corrects: 'no less than' correctly renders 'οὐχ ἧττον'; no error.

last_rejected.quote: it is not holy to wound yourself before healing another
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ὅσιον ἑαυτὸν τιτρώσκειν πρὸ τῆς θεραπείας ἑτέρου
last_rejected.why: English 'before healing another' implies temporal sequence, but Greek 'πρὸ τῆς θεραπείας ἑτέρου' means 'prior to/preferentially over the healing of another' or 'instead of healing another'. The sense is 'it is not right to wound oneself rather than heal another' or 'before one heals another' — actually 'πρό' + genitive can mean 'before' temporally or 'in preference to'. The context suggests: getting angry wounds oneself, and one shouldn't wound oneself instead of healing the other. The English 'before' captures temporal priority but misses the 'instead of' nuance. However, 'before' can mean 'rather than' in older English. In modern English, 'before' is primarily temporal. This could mislead.
last_rejected.fix: it is not right to wound yourself rather than heal another
last_rejected.ruling: 'πρὸ τῆς θεραπείας' naturally means 'before healing'; 'before' can also imply priority. Within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: the one who has fallen ill involuntarily
last_rejected.why: 'ἀκουσίως' means 'unwillingly, involuntarily' — but in context of sin/discipline, this refers to the disciple who sinned unintentionally or under compulsion. 'Involuntarily' is linguistically correct but 'unwillingly' or 'against his will' might be clearer. However, 'involuntarily' is within normal range. Not an error.
last_rejected.ruling: 'ἀκουσίως' = 'involuntarily'; reporter admits it is within normal range. No error.
